resolved_by: The Supreme Court resolved the split in United States v. Taylor, 596 U.S. 845 (2022), holding that attempted Hobbs Act robbery is not a crime of violence under § 924(c) because an attempt must itself involve actual, attempted, or threatened force.
issue: Is an attempt to commit a crime of violence automatically a crime of violence under the force clause of 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), or must the attempt itself involve the attempted use of force?

sides.position: Any attempt to commit a crime of violence is invariably a crime of violence under § 924(c) (the pre-Taylor majority view).
cases: United States v. Walker, 990 F.3d 316 (3d Cir. 2021)
United States v. Smith, 957 F.3d 590 (5th Cir. 2020)
United States v. Ingram, 947 F.3d 1021 (7th Cir. 2020)
United States v. Dominguez, 954 F.3d 1251 (9th Cir. 2020)
United States v. St. Hubert, 909 F.3d 335 (11th Cir. 2018)

sides.position: An attempt is a crime of violence under the force clause only if the attempt itself involves actual, attempted, or threatened force; an attempt to threaten force is not an attempt to use force.
cases: United States v. Taylor, 979 F.3d 203 (4th Cir. 2020), aff'd, 596 U.S. 845 (2022)
United States v. Taybron, No. 21-4358 (4th Cir. 2024)

this_court: Follows the Supreme Court's Taylor decision, holding that an attempt must itself involve attempted force to qualify under § 924(c)'s force clause.
quote: Our decision in Taylor created a split with our sister circuits, and the Supreme Court promptly took up the case.
cite: United States v. Ryan Taybron, No. 21-4358 (4th Cir. 2024)
